abstract.text:
We focus on the utilisation of reactive trajectory imitation controllers for goal-directed
mobile robot navigation. We propose a topological navigation graph (TNG) - an imitationlearning-based framework for navigating through environments with intersecting trajectories.
The TNG framework represents the environment as a directed graph composed of deep
neural networks. Each vertex of the graph corresponds to a trajectory and is represented
by a trajectory identification classifier and a trajectory imitation controller. For trajectory
following, we propose the novel use of neural object detection architectures. The edges of
TNG correspond to intersections between trajectories and are all represented by a classifier.
We provide empirical evaluation of the proposed navigation framework and its components
in simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating that TNG allows us to utilise
non-goal-directed, imitation-learning methods for goal-directed autonomous navigation.

targets.cited_work: End-to-end reinforcement-learning and metric/geometric navigation approaches.
targets.why: It avoids large joint training and precise metric localization by using modular reactive skills and minimal topological localization.
It critiques their sensitivity to rotational errors and environmental changes and their cascading-error risk.

thesis.text: A topological navigation graph can compose separately learned, non-goal-directed trajectory imitation controllers and trajectory/intersection classifiers into a goal-directed autonomous robot navigation system, with object-detection-based controllers improving robustness over regression controllers.

sections.summary: Defines trajectory following as visuomotor imitation yt=f(Xt|θ), collects expert camera-command pairs, and compares two controllers. The regression controller uses a fixed CNN encoder plus trainable MLP, ridge loss, Adam, DAgger and augmentation. It is sensitive to rotational errors and environmental change. The object-detection controller uses RetinaNet to detect a single bounding box for the robot's direction of movement, then a PID controller centers it. This recovers from larger rotational errors and can avoid low-confidence detections.

sections.summary: Reviews related topological and end-to-end navigation methods and their limitations (resource-heavy, hard assumptions, manual low-level control, no real-world demos). Then formalizes TNG as a directed graph G=(V,E): vertices are trajectory controllers plus trajectory classifiers, edges are intersection classifiers. It supports topological localization, goal identification via g(X*|φi), shortest path planning, switching controllers at intersections, and goal-reaching function.

sections.summary: Describes how classifiers, intersection detectors, goal-reaching, and trajectory controllers are implemented. Trajectory classifiers use MobileNetV2-based MLP with SoftMax, cross-entropy, fixed ImageNet encoder. Intersections and goal-reaching use a proprietary object recognition engine with FAST corners and BRIEF descriptors. Regression controller uses a 2048-1024-256-32-2 MLP with clipped output; object-detection controller uses RetinaNet and PID with clipped output.

sections.summary: Evaluates controllers in three real environments (L1-L2 office, L3 shopping centre) and one simulated environment (L4). Data collected by driving robot three times per trajectory, recording front RGB images and motor commands. Controllers trained, run for 10 laps, human interventions timed. Percentage autonomy used. Results: both nearly perfect in simulation; real-world lower; regression controller degrades more after 4 weeks than object-detection controller. Object-detection controller better tolerates environmental change and needs less aggregated data.

sections.summary: Tests TNG in an office with five trajectories T1-T5. Random initial/goal positions for each trajectory pair; autonomous navigation episodes record percentage autonomy, traveled distance, and initial/goal/final images. Results indicate TNG enables goal-directed navigation from pre-trained reactive controllers in real-world environments. Discussion contrasts TNG with metric/topological/hybrid approaches: TNG provides only minimal localization needed to keep/switch behavior. Advantages: incremental augmentation and modular perception/action selection. Limitations: assumes separable intersecting trajectories, may not handle arbitrary coverings or parallel trajectories; geometrically sub-optimal; requires human effort. But many realistic scenarios satisfy assumption.
